Title: Observed humidity trends in dry regions contradict climate models

Title: DRAFT - Data Justification Memo for California's Fifth Climate Change Assessment: Climate Adjusted Synthetic Relative Humidity Data
Short summary: The Pyregence team's own justification for replacing downscaled RH with a statistically derived synthetic product, plus full model specification and data access.
Key findings / data quality issue: Motivation: over the 2000-2020 overlap, GCM-simulated RH is significantly wetter than observed, and observed California RH has a declining trend that the simulations do not reproduce - so fire models calibrated on observations project immediately decreasing fire activity regardless of scenario. KEY CLAIM FOR PHASE 2: the authors argue bias correction can adjust modest discrepancies in mean or variance but CANNOT correct differences in long-term trends, which is why they rebuilt RH rather than correcting it. Authors' own stated limitations: the model omits large-scale atmospheric moisture transport, underestimates wet extremes of daily max RH, and has no dew point representation so max RH never spikes to 100%. They state the impact is muted for fire models because those are most sensitive to daily MINIMUM RH. Model skill: ~66% of variance explained for rmin, ~45% for rmax. Authors explicitly caution other sectors to assess suitability before using it as a replacement.
Datasets: Pyregence synthetic RH; source data = ERA5 WRF (1950-2021), UCLA WRF bias-corrected, LOCA2
Variables: RH (daily min/max), tmx, tmn, prc, elevation, aspect
Methods: Semiparametric GAM via bam() in R mgcv, with spline-smoothed interaction terms. RH fractions logit-transformed to unbounded variables. Final form: rmin2 ~ s(tmx,tmn,prc) + s(t90,p90) + s(elv,asp) + s(x,y). AIC-based selection on a 1M random subsample of >1bn daily observations. Windspeed and 30/60-day leading averages were tested but not retained. A day-of-year seasonal term was deliberately excluded so seasonality would emerge from the climate data.
Feeds deliverable: Phase 2 proposal (the trend-vs-bias-correction claim is directly load-bearing); RH report; data challenges page
Other notes?: Obtained Jul 2026, resolves the placeholder. Confirms Q02's reading of the input variables exactly. Still does NOT name the observational training dataset, and still documents no held-out validation - 'robust across randomly selected samples' is a stability check, not an overfitting test. Crucially it documents NO additional bias correction step on the LOCA2 or WRF-ERA5 inputs, so the large LOCA2 bias shift Q02 observed remains unexplained. Data access via ungoliant.ucmerced.edu (era5wrf/, wrf_bc/, loca2/) as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs. Relevance raised from Medium to High.

Title: Evaluation of the Mountain Hydroclimate across the Western United States in Dynamically Downscaled Climate Models
Short citation: Adhikari, Geerts, Rahimi-Esfarjani, Smith, Shuman & Schneider 2024 (J. Hydrometeorol. 25(12), 1877-1894)
Short summary: Evaluates how well the WUS-D3 WRF downscaling reproduces observed hydroclimate over complex terrain in the western US.
Key findings / data quality issue: Evaluates 15 CMIP6 GCMs downscaled to 9 km (WUS-D3) against PRISM, gauge/station data and a snow reanalysis over 1981-2014 for orographic precipitation, surface temperature and SWE, plus ERA5-driven 9 km and 4 km (CONUS404) reconstructions. Perkins skill for precipitation exceeds 0.9 over plains but is lower over mountains. KEY FOR THE PILLAR: it flags that gridded observational estimates in complex terrain are poorly quantified (esp. PRISM precip over mountains) - the reference-data uncertainty problem that complicates bias correction and validation in exactly the terrain where wind is also hardest.
Datasets: WRF WUS-D3 (9 km); ERA5-driven WRF (9 km + CONUS404 4 km)
Methods: Perkins skill score vs PRISM, gauge/station data and snow reanalysis; mountains-vs-plains contrast
Feeds deliverable: Good/bad matrix (complex-terrain rows); data challenges page; Phase 2 reference-dataset scoping
Other notes?: WRF WUS-D3 evaluation, not a bias-correction method paper. Rahimi-Esfarjani = Stefan Rahimi (WUS-D3 lead). Its complex-terrain reference-uncertainty finding is the most transferable point for the wind pilot and for reference-dataset choice.

Title: RH Sensitivity Analysis Plan for Cal-Adapt: AE
Short summary: The parent plan governing AE's RH bias work. Defines the goals, a three-tier use-case triage, and three workstreams: historical climatology, Heat Index, and FFWI.
Key findings / data quality issue: Framing document rather than results. Premise: CMIP6 GCMs project more near-surface moisture than observed, likely propagating into downscaled CCA5 data; affects both WRF and LOCA2; errors largest in arid regions and in the hot/dry season. Target output is a three-tier triage of use cases — proceed as-is / adjustment recommended / adjustment critically necessary — plus a feasibility assessment of an actual adjustment procedure. Datasets: WRF, LOCA2 (CCA5), ERA5, HadISD stations, AE airport station locations
Variables: RH, air temperature, dewpoint temperature, Heat Index, FFWI
Methods: Station-based comparison of WRF/LOCA2 vs ERA5 by region and IOU territory; RH derived from HadISD air temp + dewpoint to test a point-based adjustment, then generalized to gridded data; stepwise regional perturbation of RH holding physical consistency with temperature; recalculation of derived metrics (Rothfusz Heat Index, NOAA FFWI) and of threshold/exceedance metrics

Title: Personal communication on LOCA2 CA hybrid wind speed construction
Short citation: D. Pierce (Scripps), pers. comm., August 2026 [confirm exact date]
Short summary: Scripps confirmation of how wspeed is constructed and bias-corrected relative to uas/vas.
Key findings / data quality issue: wspeed is produced by averaging hourly wind speeds to daily (scalar, positive-definite), downscaled and bias-corrected separately from the vector components (signed, can cancel), with different extreme-value handling. Therefore wspeed != sqrt(uas^2+vas^2) by design. Recommendation: use the downscaled wspeed directly; do not reconstruct from daily vector winds. Resolves DQ4.
Methods: Separate downscaling + bias correction of scalar speed vs vector components
Feeds deliverable: wspeed variable card; DQ4 resolution; data challenges page
Other notes?: Personal communication; key quote retained in project notes. Fill exact email date.

Title: Cal-Adapt downscaled products vs ERA5: 10 m wind agreement over California (v2)
Short summary: Head-to-head validation of AE downscaled 10 m wind (LOCA2 statistical + WRF dynamical, same GCM) vs ERA5 over California, 1980-2010.
Key findings / data quality issue: Both products run high vs ERA5 with agreeing timing (seasonal r 0.77-0.92) and a multiplicative offset. On 1351 shared cells the STATISTICAL LOCA2 (+29%) is CLOSER to ERA5 than the DYNAMICAL WRF-GCM (+69%). This REJECTS the v1 hypothesis that LOCA2's offset came from PresRat: the uncorrected dynamical product is the outlier and PresRat moves LOCA2 toward ERA5. Offset largest over flat interior terrain (opposite of a resolution effect), so origin is upstream (GCM wind climate, WRF surface/PBL, or ERA5 10m diagnostic at 31km). Big caveat: sampling frequency not matched (WRF native-timestep vs ERA5 hourly) inflates WRF. Decisive next step: WRF-ERA5 run (same sampling).
Methods: source->ERA5 block-mean regrid (rectilinear + curvilinear paths); coverage mask; ERA5 hourly->scalar->monthly; climatological metrics
Feeds deliverable: good/bad matrix (mean-bias dimension); wspeed variable card (ERA5 validation); data challenges page
Other notes?: v2 supersedes v1. Single realization each; sampling-frequency caveat on WRF. See era5-comparison page + FINDINGS_v2.md. Next: WRF-ERA5 control run.
